introduction: Part III of the Indian Constitution (Articles 12 to 35) deals with Fundamental Rights. Inspired by the 'Bill of Rights' of the USA, these rights are essential for the intellectual, moral, and spiritual development of citizens. Part III is rightly described as the 'Magna Carta' of India.

core_concepts.title: The 6 Fundamental Rights
core_concepts.description: Originally there were 7 rights, but currently there are 6: 1. Right to Equality (14-18), 2. Right to Freedom (19-22), 3. Right against Exploitation (23-24), 4. Right to Freedom of Religion (25-28), 5. Cultural and Educational Rights (29-30), 6. Right to Constitutional Remedies (32).

core_concepts.title: Right to Property
core_concepts.description: Originally a Fundamental Right under Article 31. However, the 44th Constitutional Amendment Act (1978) removed it from the list of Fundamental Rights and made it a 'Legal Right' under Article 300A in Part XII.

core_concepts.title: Article 32 (Constitutional Remedies)
core_concepts.description: This article allows a citizen to directly approach the Supreme Court if their Fundamental Rights are violated. Without this article, all other rights would be meaningless as there would be no way to enforce them.

important_entities.name: Dr. B.R. Ambedkar
important_entities.significance: He famously called Article 32 the 'Heart and Soul of the Constitution'.

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.alert_title: Right to Property is NOT a Fundamental Right
trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: Students often get confused here. Always remember that the Right to Property is now only a Constitutional/Legal right, not a Fundamental Right. It was deleted by the 44th Amendment in 1978.

mnemonics_and_tricks.memory_phrase: E-F-E-R-C-R (Every Friday Everyone Reads Current affairs Regularly)
mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: Equality, Freedom, Exploitation, Religion, Cultural/Educational, Remedies.

exam_strategy_tips: Questions asking which country we borrowed Fundamental Rights from (Answer: USA) are very common.
Which part of the Constitution is called the 'Magna Carta of India'? (Answer: Part III).
